_note: Cambridge B2 First — Reading and Use of English, Part 1 (multiple-choice cloze), 12 gaps. Extended practice beyond the exam's 8 gaps: four original INTUITY texts, each written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (every option set kept word for word, with its keyed answer; only the context sentence is new). Paragraphs in `text` carry NUMBERED {n} placeholders matched to the question whose `number` is n, so a renderer never counts gaps. Each question carries `focus`, `why` and a note per distractor, so a student learns the pattern, not just the answer.
title: Reading and Use of English — Part 1
timing: The whole paper is 1 hour 15 minutes. In the exam Part 1 has 8 gaps worth 8 marks of 52; these 12-gap texts are extended practice, so allow about 15 minutes each.
rubric: For questions 1–12, read the text below and decide which answer (A, B, C or D) best fits each gap. There is an example at the beginning (0).

tests.title: Treading the grapes
tests.source: Original INTUITY text, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (2.14 3.11 4.17 5.5 5.6 1.17 5.3 5.12 3.1 3.6 2.5 2.9)
text: Every autumn, the hill village of Valdoro marks the end of the grape season with a festival that visitors rarely forget. The celebration {0} place on the last Saturday of September, once the farmers have finished helping one another to {1} the grapes on the steep hillsides. {2} 1890, the high point of the day has been the treading of the fruit in huge wooden tubs in the main square.

Anyone is welcome to join in, {3} they do not mind getting rather sticky. Participants climb into the tubs with {4} feet and stamp on the grapes to the sound of drums, while the crowd cheers them on. There is no age {5}, and it is not unusual to see a grandmother sharing a tub with a five-year-old. Last year more than three thousand people {6} the festival, and there was hardly enough {7} in the square for everyone to stand.

As darkness falls, long tables are {8} with plates of bread, cheese and grilled vegetables, and the whole village eats together beneath lanterns in {9} colours. Just before midnight, each child is given a single grape and told to {10} a wish. Broadly {11}, the wine made from the trodden grapes is not the best the region produces, but nobody seems to mind. The date of next year's festival has not been announced {12}, but the village's few guesthouses are already fully booked.

example.why: An event takes place, meaning it happens. 'Makes', 'has' and 'gives' do not combine with 'place' in this sense.

questions.why: You harvest grapes, wheat or other crops when you gather them in at the end of the season.

distractors.transfer: means to move something from one place to another, not to pick it
distractors.empty: is done to containers, not to plants

questions.why: 'Since' + a point in time, followed by the present perfect, shows when something started and that it continues now.

distractors.As: cannot be followed by a year on its own
distractors.While: needs a clause or a period, not a single year
distractors.Because: gives a reason and cannot be followed by a year

questions.why: 'Providing' means 'on condition that': you may join if you accept getting sticky.

distractors.despite: must be followed by a noun or -ing form, not a clause
distractors.unless: reverses the meaning: you could join only if you did mind

questions.why: Feet with no shoes or socks on are bare feet.

distractors.free: 'free feet' is not an English expression
distractors.clear: does not describe feet without shoes
distractors.open: does not describe feet without shoes

questions.why: An age limit is the highest or lowest age allowed to take part.

distractors.lip: is the edge of a cup or a mouth
distractors.edge: is the side of a physical object
distractors.outline: is a shape or a short plan

questions.why: To attend an event is to go to it; 'attend' takes a direct object.

distractors.looked: needs a preposition and means to use your eyes
distractors.cared: needs 'about' or 'for' and means to feel concern

questions.why: 'Room' is uncountable space that is free to be used: enough room to stand.

distractors.interval: is a gap in time, or the break in a play
distractors.range: is a variety or a distance, not free space
distractors.extent: is the size or degree of something

questions.why: A table is set (or laid) with plates and food when it is prepared for a meal.

distractors.established: means to start an organisation or system
distractors.founded: is used for starting companies, schools or towns
distractors.placed: would mean the tables were put down somewhere, and does not take 'with plates'

questions.why: Strong, cheerful colours are bright colours.

distractors.sharp: describes edges, pain or images, not colours
distractors.high: describes height or levels, not colours

questions.why: In English you make a wish.

distractors.order: is used for food or goods you want to buy
distractors.prepare: is used for meals or plans
distractors.form: is used for groups or opinions, not wishes

questions.why: 'Broadly speaking' is a fixed phrase meaning 'in general'.

distractors.telling: does not form a fixed phrase with 'broadly'
distractors.saying: does not form a fixed phrase with 'broadly'
distractors.talking: does not form a fixed phrase with 'broadly'

questions.why: 'Not ... yet' at the end of a negative sentence means it has not happened so far but is expected.

distractors.just: does not go at the end of a negative sentence like this
distractors.even: cannot stand at the end of the clause
distractors.already: is used in positive sentences, not with 'not' here

tests.title: Miss Hartley's machines
tests.source: Original INTUITY text, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (2.13 3.15 2.8 4.13 2.6 1.9 3.12 1.10 1.3 1.20 1.16 4.10)
text: Edith Hartley {0} up in the rooms above her father's clock shop in a small northern town. As a child she was so shy that her teachers said she was afraid of her own {1}, yet at home she never stopped asking {2}. Why did a clock tick? What made a spring jump back? Her father's only piece of {3} to her was simple: 'Take everything apart, but remember where each piece goes.' {4} formed in childhood are hard to break, and Edith never lost that one.

By the age of thirty she had filled forty notebooks with {5} for new machines, from a gate that closed itself to a kettle that whistled a tune. Many of them looked clever on paper, but she soon discovered that making them work in {6} was much harder. When she showed her washing machine at a London exhibition in 1932, she {7} a group of engineers laughing at the woman in the plain grey coat. She remained perfectly {8}, however, and calmly switched the machine on. The audience watched in stunned {9} as it washed and dried a basket of shirts in under an hour, and one journalist {10} on how quietly it ran.

Today Edith's designs are highly {11} by engineers, and several are on display in a museum. When an interviewer once asked her the secret of her success, she replied that she had {12} her childhood dream simply by never being too shy to ask 'why?'

example.why: 'Grow up' means to spend your childhood somewhere. 'Raised' and 'brought (up)' need a passive here (was brought up), and 'rose' means went higher.

questions.why: Someone who is 'afraid of their own shadow' is extremely timid; it is a fixed expression.

distractors.shade: is an area out of the sun, not the dark shape that follows you
distractors.screen: is a flat surface for showing pictures

questions.why: You ask questions; this is the natural, everyday collocation.

distractors.enquiries: are made, not asked, and sound formal
distractors.queries: are raised, and suggest doubts about something official
distractors.investigations: are carried out, usually by police or experts

questions.why: 'Advice' is uncountable, so one item of it is 'a piece of advice'.

distractors.mind: the phrase is 'peace of mind', which means calm
distractors.suggestion: is countable, so you cannot say 'a piece of suggestion'
distractors.statement: is countable, and a statement is not guidance

questions.why: Habits are formed and are hard to break; the verbs 'form' and 'break' collocate with 'habit'.

distractors.Means: are ways of doing something, and are not 'broken'
distractors.Methods: are ways of working, not things you break
distractors.Procedures: are official steps, not things formed in childhood

questions.why: Plans for things you might invent are ideas.

distractors.views: are opinions about a subject, not plans for machines
distractors.opinions: are what you think about something, not designs
distractors.beliefs: are things you hold to be true

questions.why: 'In practice' means in reality, contrasted here with 'on paper'.

distractors.action: 'in action' means while doing something, not in reality
distractors.operation: 'in operation' means working or running, which repeats 'work'

questions.why: To notice someone doing something is to see it and become aware of it; 'notice' takes an object + -ing.

distractors.remarked: means said, and is followed by 'on' or 'that'

questions.why: A person who stays calm under pressure remains composed.

distractors.put up: is a phrasal verb, not an adjective describing calm
distractors.settled: describes weather, a home or a decision, not calm under pressure

questions.why: 'In stunned disbelief' describes being so surprised you can hardly believe what you see.

distractors.uncertainty: does not combine with 'stunned' to show amazement

questions.why: 'Remark on' means to make a comment about something.

distractors.observed: takes a direct object or 'that', not 'on'

questions.why: 'Highly regarded' means greatly respected.

distractors.believed: does not combine with 'highly' in this sense
distractors.judged: does not combine with 'highly' to mean respected

questions.why: You fulfil a dream, an ambition or a wish when you make it come true.

distractors.occupied: is used for space or time
distractors.possessed: means owned, and does not combine with 'dream'
distractors.covered: means put something over, or dealt with a topic

tests.title: The sun boats
tests.source: Original INTUITY text, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (1.1 1.4 4.18 4.7 4.2 1.12 2.17 5.10 3.17 5.11 2.2 4.1)
text: When the town council of Marren decided to replace its old diesel ferries, few people {0} the idea seriously. Fuel prices were {1}, the boats were noisy, and they rarely ran {2} time. Then a local engineer, Tom Brannock, came up with a boat powered entirely by the sun. The electricity {3} by the panels on its roof was stored in batteries, so it could cross the lake even on cloudy days. After {4} the cost of each boat at around forty thousand pounds, far less than a new ferry, he took his plans to the council.

Today the council operates a {5} of six sun boats, which carry passengers between the villages around the lake. Because there is a strict {6} limit on the water to protect the swans, they travel slowly, but nobody seems to mind. The lake is noticeably cleaner, and scientists have recorded a {7} improvement in the number of fish. The boats need very little attention, although every few years the council must {8} the batteries checked.

Brannock admits he was more than {9} with the result. When a national television {10} showed a documentary about the boats, so many visitors asked for the little guidebook about them that the council had to print two thousand extra {11} of it. Towns from as far away as Norway have since made {12} with Brannock, hoping to build sun boats of their own.

example.why: To take something seriously is a fixed phrase meaning to treat it as important. 'Made', 'gave' and 'held' do not form this phrase.

questions.why: Prices are high or low in English.

distractors.wide: describes width or a range, not prices
distractors.large: is used for sizes and amounts, not prices

questions.why: 'On time' means at the correct, planned time.

distractors.for: 'for time' is not a phrase about punctuality
distractors.by: 'by time' is not English in this sense
distractors.at: 'at time' is not English; you say 'at the right time'

questions.why: Electricity is produced (generated) by solar panels.

distractors.built: is used for structures, not electricity
distractors.done: is used for tasks, not energy
distractors.shaped: means given a form, which electricity does not have

questions.why: To estimate a cost at a figure is to calculate it roughly.

distractors.balancing: means keeping things equal, not guessing a figure
distractors.numbering: means giving things numbers in order
distractors.counting: means adding up one by one and does not take 'at' a figure

questions.why: A group of boats, ships or vehicles owned by one organisation is a fleet.

distractors.staff: means the people who work somewhere
distractors.crew: means the people who work on a boat, not the boats
distractors.set: is used for matching objects like cups or tools, not boats

questions.why: A speed limit is the fastest you are allowed to travel.

distractors.hurry: does not form a compound with 'limit'
distractors.rush: does not form a compound with 'limit'
distractors.dash: does not form a compound with 'limit'

questions.why: 'A marked improvement' is a clear, noticeable one.

distractors.sore: describes a painful part of the body
distractors.hurt: describes a person who is injured or upset

questions.why: 'Get something done' means to arrange for someone else to do it.

distractors.let: would need a bare infinitive: let the batteries be checked
distractors.make: would need an active infinitive: make someone check

questions.why: You are pleased with a result; 'more than pleased' means very happy.

distractors.rewarded: means given something for good work, and is not used with 'more than ... with'
distractors.persuaded: means made to agree, which does not fit the meaning

questions.why: Programmes are shown on a television channel.

distractors.life: does not combine with 'television' in this way
distractors.world: 'the television world' means the industry, which does not show programmes
distractors.area: is a part of a place, not a broadcaster

questions.why: Individual examples of the same book or magazine are copies.

distractors.prints: are copies of photos or paintings, not guidebooks
distractors.pages: are parts of a book, not whole books for visitors

questions.why: 'Make contact with' someone means to communicate with them for the first time.

distractors.touch: the phrase is 'get in touch with', not 'make touch'
distractors.general: does not form a phrase with 'make ... with'
distractors.common: 'make common cause' is a different, formal phrase

tests.title: The Blue Kettle
tests.source: Original INTUITY text, written around the teacher's own calibrated option sets (3.4 5.9 4.3 2.19 2.20 1.11 4.8 4.6 1.7 3.10 4.5 1.19)
text: The Blue Kettle has been {0} by the same family for sixty years. It stands on a steep, narrow street in Pellow, a fishing village {1} the market town of Brindle, and it is by no {2} the smartest café on the coast. The chairs do not match, the windows rattle in the wind, and there is only one waitress, Rosa, who squeezes between the tables {3} a heavy tray in each hand. Yet people travel from all over the country to visit it, and the reason is a book.

A best-selling novel, {4} in Pellow in the 1950s, opens with a famous scene in which a fisherman {5} his fist on a café table and swears he will never go to sea again. {6} the author never revealed which café she was {7} to, the Blue Kettle has happily claimed the honour for itself.

Over the years, most visitors have {8} exactly the same meal as the fisherman, a bowl of fish soup with thick brown bread. Some even ask Rosa to {9} the question that has puzzled readers for decades: did he ever go back to sea? Rosa, who has long {10} that the mystery is good for business, only smiles. She will happily tell you her {11} for keeping the old chairs, however. 'They have heard more stories than I have,' she says. If you would like a table by the window in summer, it is wise to {12} the café a call a few days in advance.

example.why: You run a business such as a café or a shop. 'Led' is for groups of people, 'held' for events or positions, and 'driven' for vehicles.

questions.why: 'Near' means not far from a place.

distractors.on: would put the village on top of the town
distractors.about: means around inside a place, not close to it
distractors.over: means above or across, not close to

questions.why: 'By no means' is a fixed phrase meaning 'not at all'.

distractors.process: does not form a fixed phrase with 'by no'
distractors.system: does not form a fixed phrase with 'by no'
distractors.method: does not form a fixed phrase with 'by no'

questions.why: To carry something is to hold it while you move.

distractors.fetching: means going to get something and bringing it back, not holding it as you move
distractors.reaching: means stretching out a hand, and needs 'for'
distractors.sitting: does not take an object like 'a tray'

questions.why: A story is set in the place and time where it happens.

distractors.placed: is not used for the setting of a story
distractors.put: is not used for the setting of a story

questions.why: You bang your fist on a table when you hit it hard in anger.

distractors.ground: means crushed or rubbed, not hit
distractors.cracked: means broke slightly; you crack a cup, not your fist on a table
distractors.broken: is a past participle and cannot be the main verb here

questions.why: 'Since' at the start of a sentence gives a reason, like 'because'.

distractors.out of: must be followed by a noun, e.g. 'out of curiosity'
distractors.so: introduces a result and cannot begin this kind of sentence
distractors.owing to: must be followed by a noun, not a clause

questions.why: To refer to something is to mean or mention it.

distractors.working: 'work to' a café makes no sense

questions.why: In a café or restaurant you order food.

distractors.noticed: means saw, not asked for food
distractors.told: needs a person as its object

questions.why: You answer a question.

distractors.satisfy: is used for needs or people, not a question
distractors.match: means to be equal or similar to something
distractors.serve: is used for food, customers or a purpose

questions.why: To sense that something is true is to feel or realise it without being told.

distractors.experienced: is followed by a noun, not a 'that' clause
distractors.lived: cannot be followed by a 'that' clause
distractors.had: cannot be followed by a 'that' clause

questions.why: Your reasons for doing something explain why you do it; 'reason' takes 'for'.

distractors.purposes: means aims, and does not take 'for' + -ing like this
distractors.intentions: are plans for the future, not explanations

questions.why: 'Give someone a call' means to phone them.

distractors.get: 'get a call' means receive one, and cannot take 'the café' as well
distractors.take: 'take a call' means answer the phone, not make the call
